You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The current bug report describes that default arguments only work if no arguments are submitted, leading to counter-intuitive behavior where defaults are only picked up if no arguments are passed in. Looking at the failing test `testSingleOptionMaximumNumberOfArgument`, the test sets up an option `"b"` with a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 4 arguments, along with default values "100", "1000", and "10000". The test then parses an array of arguments `["-b", "1", "2"]` and expects the values for option `-b` to be `[1, 2, 10000]`.

The issue in the bug report aligns with the failing test's behavior as the test only expects the default values to be picked when no arguments are passed in. This suggests that the handling of default values in the parser's parsing logic may be incorrect.

To delve deeper into the root cause, we need to inspect the implementation of the parser and how it handles default values when parsing arguments.

Let's examine relevant methods in the codebase to understand how default values are processed during parsing.

messages.content:
The `DefaultOptionBuilder` class has a `reset` method that resets various properties of the option being built, including the `preferredName`, `description`, `aliases`, `required`, `argument`, and more. This method is used to clean the state of the builder for a new option configuration.

On the other hand, the `DefaultOption` class defines the constructor that initializes the default option with various parameters, such as `shortPrefix`, `longPrefix`, `burstEnabled`, `preferredName`, `description`, `aliases`, `burstAliases`, `required`, `argument`, `children`, and `id`. This constructor sets up the option with the provided values and configurations.

Given this information, the issue with default arguments behavior might be related to how the default values are processed and set in the `DefaultOption` class constructor or during the parser's argument parsing logic. There could be a discrepancy in handling default values when arguments are provided, resulting in the observed counter-intuitive behavior where defaults are only picked up if no arguments are passed.

To address this issue, it could be necessary to review the logic in the `DefaultOption` class related to handling default values and ensure that defaults are correctly processed even when arguments are provided. Additional investigation into the parser's parsing logic might also be needed to ensure proper handling of default values in all scenarios.

Here are the methods that could be potential locations for fixing the issue:
1. `org.apache.commons.cli2.DefaultOption.DefaultOption(java.lang.String, java.lang.String, boolean, java.lang.String, java.lang.String, java.util.Set, java.util.Set, boolean, org.apache.commons.cli2.Argument, org.apache.commons.cli2.Group, int)`
2. `org.apache.commons.cli2.Parser.parse(java.lang.String[])`
